content.title: Chuck Norris, Bruce Lee co-star and martial arts icon, dies at 86
content.text: It’s one of the most iconic moments in Bruce Lee’s brief filmography. Set in the Roman Colosseum, site of so much ancient gladiatorial combat, two martial artists battle to the death in the climax of the 1972 action classic “The Way of the Dragon.” One of them, of course, is Lee, the San Francisco-born icon who was starring in and making his directorial debut. The other was a disciple of Lee’s named Chuck Norris, an accomplished martial artist in his own right who was appearing in his first major film role.  Norris would later shoot to fame as the bearded action star of the 1980s in films such as “Missing in Action” and “Delta Force” and as the lead in the durable television series “Walker, Texas Ranger.” He also became a bestselling author and continued acting until his death at age 86 on Thursday, March 19, on Kauai, Hawaii. Norris celebrated his birthday just over a week before his death, posting a sparring video on Instagram. “I don’t age,” he wrote. “I level up.” His family members described his death on social media as a “sudden passing” and requested privacy. They noted “he was surrounded by his family and was at peace.” Born Carlos Ray Norris in Ryan, Okla., on March 10, 1940, Norris moved with his family at age 12 to the Southern California beachside town of Torrance (Los Angeles County). He joined the U.S. Air Force at age 18 and began training in martial arts during a deployment to South Korea. By the mid-1960s he was a black belt in several martial arts disciplines and was an instructor to Hollywood celebrities — among them Bob Barker, Priscilla Presley, Donny and Marie Osmond, and Steve McQueen.  It was McQueen, star of 1968’s San Francisco-shot “Bullitt,” who urged him to become an actor. Norris made his onscreen debut in “The Wrecking Crew” (1969), in which he is defeated by secret agent Matt Helm (Dean Martin) in a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it moment. But it was with his association with Lee that helped him turn the corner. When Norris was dominating the All-American Karate Championship with a string of titles in the mid-1960s, Lee was co-starring as Kato in the ABC series “The Green Hornet.” They became friends and training partners. After Lee’s death, Norris parlayed his success in “The Way of the Dragon” — the top-grossing Hong Kong film of 1972 — into the main villain role in a 1974 Hong Kong hit, “Yellow Faced Tiger,” in which he plays a San Francisco drug lord. In 1981, during the early stages of Norris’ stardom, the film was reedited and released under the title “Slaughter in San Francisco.” Norris first became known to American audiences in “Breaker! Breaker!” (1977), a modest hit, and “Good Guys Wear Black” (1978), a solid success that made him a bankable star. He would then star in a string of hits, including “A Force of One” (1979), “The Octagon” (1980) and “An Eye for an Eye” (1981). Those films helped land him a lucrative contract with upstart studio Cannon Films, which made him an A-list international star in films such as “Missing in Action” (1984), “Invasion U.S.A.” (1985) and “The Delta Force” (1986), a cult classic about an airplane hostage crisis that co-starred Lee Marvin. Norris became a part of a wave of action heroes during that era, joining the ranks of Sylvester Stallone, Arnold Schwarzenegger and Jean-Claude Van Damme, who were unashamedly the good guys. This was in contrast to the 1970s, when action heroes — such as Clint Eastwood’s Dirty Harry — were often morally shaded. “I wanted to project a certain image on the screen of a hero,” Norris said in 1982. “I had seen a lot of antihero movies in which the lead was neither good nor bad. There was no one to root for.” That hero persona continued in “Walker, Texas Ranger,” which ran for nine seasons on CBS (1993-2001). After the series’ cancellation, he continued acting and became a spokesperson for Total Home Gym in a series of infomercials. He was also active in Christian causes and conservative politics and published books, co-writing the novel “The Justice Riders” (2006) and the nonfiction “Black Belt Patriotism: How to Reawaken America” (2008). Then there were the first internet memes.  “Chuck Norris Facts” went viral online with such wildly hyperbolic statements as, “Chuck Norris had a staring contest with the sun — and won,” and, “They wanted to put Chuck Norris on Mt. Rushmore, but the granite wasn’t tough enough for his beard.” His last major film role came in “The Expendables 2” (2012). At the time of his death, he had completed a small role in “Zombie Plane,” an action comedy that is expected to be released later this year. Norris is survived by his wife, Gena Norris, and five children: stunt performers Mike and Eric with his late ex-wife, Dianne Holechek; twins Dakota and Danilee with Gena Norris; and Dina, the result of an early 1960s “one-night stand” revealed in his autobiography. The Associated Press contributed to this report.
